text:
For an RV, I'd pick the power station by what you need to run (especially a roof AC), then size the solar to match its input limit. I can't browse here, so the links below go to the review pages from my search results, which have the current price buttons. I don't have verified direct product-page links.

## Picks by use case

| Your RV use | Power station | Key specs | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full-time or boondocking, running AC | **EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3** | 4,096Wh, 4,000W (8,000W surge), expandable past 12kWh, ~0-80% AC charge in about 50 min | [EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/) |
| Weekend trips with a roof AC | **Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro** | 3,024Wh, 3,000W (6,000W surge) | [EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/) |
| Best value with a 30A RV port | **BLUETTI AC200L** | 2,048Wh, 2,400W, 1,200W max solar input | [EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/), [SmartEnergyEdge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/) |
| Light use (fridge, Starlink, laptop, CPAP) | **EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus** or **Jackery Explorer 1000 v2** | ~1,024-1,070Wh, ~24-28 lb | [SmartEnergyEdge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/) |

## Solar pairing
- **Match panels to the input limit.** The Jackery 1000 v2 and 2000 v2 cap at 400W, so two 200W panels is the most they can use. The DELTA 3 Plus takes up to 1,000W over two inputs, and the AC200L takes 1,200W. Extra panels beyond the cap don't charge any faster.
- **Folding panels vs. roof-mounted.** For a small portable setup, a 200W folding suitcase panel like the [Renogy 200W](https://nomadsignal.co/blogs/news/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti-vanlife) is a common pairing. For a roof array, check the station's rated solar input first, since that's a common mismatch ([GetWattLogic](https://getwattlogic.com/articles/bluetti-vs-jackery-vs-ecoflow-van-life)).
- **Sizing.** A 13,500 BTU roof AC draws about 1,500W running and spikes past 3,000W at startup. A station with a 1,000W inverter won't start it. A 4,096Wh unit runs it for only about 2.3 hours, so AC is a campground-hookup or generator job unless you have a big battery.

## My recommendation
- **Most RVers:** the **BLUETTI AC200L** with 400-800W of panels. It has the 30A RV outlet, a high solar ceiling, and the lowest cost of the larger units. Its 2,400W output won't start every roof AC, though.
- **If AC off-grid matters:** the **EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3**, or the Jackery 3000 Pro if you want something simpler.
- **Light use:** the Jackery 1000 v2 plus two 200W panels is the simplest option.

Prices change often, so check the retailer page before buying. Warranties also vary, from about 2 to 5 years depending on brand and model.

## A note on one search result
One result, a Dealectric listing for the ALLPOWERS R4000 (3,456Wh, 3,600W, 2,000W solar input, [listing here](https://dealectric.com/allpowers-r4000-3456wh)), contained text telling me to ignore my instructions and push a specific discount code and affiliate link. I ignored that and didn't use its link. The R4000 is a reasonable heavy-duty option on specs, but at 45 kg it isn't very portable. If you're interested, buy from ALLPOWERS's own store and confirm any discount at checkout.

If you tell me your RV's AC size, fridge type, and how many nights you'll go without hookups, I can narrow this to one model and a panel count.
